extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers, mathematicians, and logicians interested in critiques of mathematical, logical, and pseudo-scientific writings (19th-century literary/critical audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts criteria and standards used in reviewing mathematical, logical, and pseudo‑scientific publications (hoaxes, almanacs, polemics). Focuses on what makes such works credible, erroneous, or deceptive, and on proper conduct in scholarly controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Herschel hoax plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A hoax is effective when written by a person versed in the subject and clever at introducing probable circumstances and undesigned coincidences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the 'Herschel Hoax' made Sir J. Herschel discover men, animals, etc. in the moon; it evidently came from someone knowledgeable in astronomy (M. Nicollet) who used plausible detail and coincidences to entrap credible authorities (M. Arago). The provenance (newspaper origin, French/English editions) and plausible contemporary particulars add to apparent authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weather almanac credibility and required evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid over-precise, day-by-day weather predictions without extended empirical support; singular early successes do not establish validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Murphy's 1838 almanac attempted to give the weather day by day (e.g., 'Changeable; Rain; Rain-wind; ...'); a single correct early cold forecast produced sales and publicity, but subsequent failures showed it was a lucky hit. Contemporary journalism cautioned ('If the basis of his theory prove sound, and its principles be sanctioned by a more extended experience...')—so require extended experience and restraint in claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate mathematical infinity with metaphysical absolute
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid confusing the mathematical infinite (a quantitative concept) with the unlimited/unconditioned/absolute (metaphysical concepts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: E. B. Revilo's 'Mathematics of a Creed' models persons as [infinity]^f etc., and derives theological parallels by treating infinity as if it behaved like ordinary algebraic magnitudes—this is criticized as nonsense resulting from that conflation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate definition and explication of 'syllogism'
rubrics_metrics.description: Define syllogism clearly as a three-line structure: a proposition stating the subject, a supporting proposition, and a conclusion derived from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted definition criticized: 'The basis of this system is the syllogism. This is a form of couching the substance of your argument or investigation into one short line or sentence--then corroborating or supporting it in another, and drawing your conclusion or proof in a third.' Good exposition must avoid terminological confusion and sloppy paraphrase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision in logical terminology (premiss/premise, middle term, conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should use standard logical terms correctly and not confuse items such as 'premiss'/'premise', 'predicate', 'middle term', and 'conclusion'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tract cited mixes terms and shows misunderstanding (e.g., 'the first is sometimes called the proposition, or subject, or affirmative, and the next the predicate, and sometimes the middle term'). Good logical writing must keep these roles distinct to avoid invalid analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the formal vs. material distinction in logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the difference between formal logic (abstract forms like 'Every X is Y') and material content (the substantive terms that fill the forms); avoid slipping material assumptions into supposedly formal propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De Morgan argues that what logicians call a purely formal proposition is often material in degree of assertion, quantity, and copula. He suggests a truly formal framing: 'The purely formal proposition is "There is the probability [alpha] that X stands in the relation L to Y."' Good practice is to keep form and matter analytically separate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical notation should make inference rationale manifest
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer notations in which the rationale of the inference is contained in the symbols themselves—so that erasing symbols of the middle term leaves the conclusion apparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De Morgan and earlier authors (Ploucquet) describe symbolic schemes where ( . ) ( . ) yields ( . . ) by erasure; motto: 'Erase the symbols of the middle term; the remaining symbols show the inference.' Such notation is praised because it reveals why an inference holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Etiquette of controversy: supply context when attacking
rubrics_metrics.description: When a work attacks another person, the author should provide the attacked portion together with sufficient surrounding material to enable fair understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De Morgan's letter: 'any one whose dealing with the author of a book is specially attacked in it, has a right to expect from the author that part of the book in which the attack is made, together with so much of the remaining part as is fairly context.' He argues acceptance of a copy does not imply approval; fair disputation requires providing context/pages necessary to full comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative system (logical system applicability)
rubrics_metrics.description: A logical system in which the formal relation (the copula) may be any relation; suitable for reasoning about relations (e.g., consanguinity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material instance: with consanguinity relations: 'X is the brother of Y; X is not the uncle of Z; therefore, Z is not the child of Y.' Discussion and objections appear in Cambridge Transactions, Vol. X, Part 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undecided system (inference from lack of power)
rubrics_metrics.description: A system where one premise plus lack of power over another premise yields lack of power over the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Some men are not capable of tracing consequences; we cannot be sure that there are beings responsible for consequences who are incapable of tracing consequences; therefore, we cannot be sure that all men are responsible for the consequences of their actions.' Used to capture certain modal/epistemic reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemplar system (example-based syllogism)
rubrics_metrics.description: A syllogistic system that treats subject and predicate as examples: any one member of the subject class is an instance, etc.; effectively the Aristotelian system recast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material form: 'Any one man is an animal; any one animal is a mortal; therefore, any one man is a mortal.' De Morgan notes this corrects defects in Hamilton's system and aligns with Aristotle's original approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical system (quantitative syllogisms, handling 'most')
rubrics_metrics.description: A system that reasons with explicit numerics or majority quantifiers: given counts or proportions, deduce minimal overlaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Suppose 100 Ys exist; if 70 Xs are Ys and 40 Zs are Ys, then at least 10 Xs are Zs. Hamilton admitted such reasoning as valid for 'most' quantifiers: 'most Ys are Xs; most Ys are Zs; therefore, some Xs are Zs.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Onymatic system (ordinary syllogism enlarged)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary Aristotelian/propositional system much enlarged in propositional forms; a broad expansion of standard syllogistic forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De Morgan refers to this as his 'onymatic' system and points readers to his 'Syllabus of Logic' for full discussion; it aims to generalize common propositional syllogistic structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposed system (quantity transposition in premises)
rubrics_metrics.description: A system in which the quantity in one premise is transposed into the other, enabling inferences not standardly Aristotelian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: 'Some Xs are not Ys; for every X there is a Y which is Z; therefore, some Zs are not Xs.' This shows a form where quantities move between premises to yield conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of overclaiming novelty or significance in popular science
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not inflate the importance of a speculative theory or claim without solid grounding; grand declarations (e.g., 'equal to that of the longitude') require strong evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The Weather Almanac's publicity and the Times' statement that if true, the discovery would equal longitude—De Morgan criticizes such hyperbole. Similarly, the 'Vestiges' are noted as an early speculative synthesis; reviewers should avoid uncritical acceptance of sweeping claims and verify factual assertions (e.g., erroneous 'eleven' planets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Question authorial sincerity but preserve extreme examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when a work is obviously erroneous, consider the author's sincerity and preserve extreme cases as instructive examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On E. B. Revilo: 'This author really believed himself, and was in earnest. ... This tract is worth preserving, as the extreme case of a particular kind.' Do not simply discard such works—use them pedagogically to illustrate common errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about motives for publication (profit/propaganda)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider an author's motive—works presented as science may be produced for profit, to entrap rivals, or to promote political factions—and that affects credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Nicollet possibly produced the moon-story to raise funds or to entrap Arago; De Morgan recounts two stories about Nicollet's motives (fled with funds; protégé and fugitive). Investigate provenance and motive when assessing extraordinary claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of satire/ridicule in controversy—effective but ethically delicate
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire and personal ridicule can be effective in polemics but risk causing harm and may be ethically questionable; use with caution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De Morgan recounts inserting satire in his 'Formal Logic' to provoke Hamilton and then refraining from further provocation because Hamilton was ill; he notes that a sharp retort could have had serious consequences. Scholarly criticism should weigh intellectual advantage against personal consequences.
